--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.transitivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute global transitivity (clustering coefficient). twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.transitivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: Compute global transitivity (clustering coefficient). title: >- [Graph.transitivity()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: Compute global transitivity (clustering coefficient). page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute global transitivity (clustering coefficient). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L35648-L35783){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.transitivity() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Transitivity](../assets/graphs/transitivity.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A five-node graph with two triangles in the accent color. Badges count the connected triples centered on each node (1, 3, 3, 3, 0), ten in all. The card computes 3 times 2 triangles over 10 triples, transitivity 0.6." width="100%"} Transitivity measures the probability that two neighbors of a node are also connected. It's computed as: `transitivity = 3 * (number of triangles) / (number of connected triples)` A connected triple is a path of length 2 (three nodes where at least two edges connect them). Higher transitivity indicates more clustering. On directed graphs, edge direction is followed: a connected triple is a directed path `u -> v -> w` through three distinct nodes, and it counts as closed when the edge `w -> u` exists, completing a directed 3-cycle. The result is the fraction of such paths that close. A path that returns to its start (`u -> v -> u`, from a pair of reciprocal edges) is not a triple, so a triangle with edges in both directions scores `1.0`. The measure is computed on the simple graph in both cases: parallel edges count once and self-loops are ignored. Returns `None` if there are no connected triples in the graph. Time complexity: `O(m * d_max)` where `m` is edges and `d_max` is maximum degree. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Optional[float]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Global clustering coefficient between `0.0` and `1.0`, or `None` if undefined. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~average_clustering_coefficient`) : The mean of each node's clustering. [](`~count_triangles`) : The number of triangles at each node. [](`~random_reference`) : A random graph with the same degrees, to compare against. ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a triangle with a tail, there are five pairs of edges that meet at a node, and three of them are closed by the third edge of the triangle, so the transitivity is 3/5: ::: {#20a6d4ed .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D")] ) graph.transitivity() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.6 ``` ::: ::: The average clustering of the same graph is 0.58. Transitivity pools every node's pairs of neighbors, so a node with many neighbors weighs more, where the average counts every node the same: ::: {#56e73265 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.average_clustering_coefficient() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 0.5833333333333333 ``` ::: ::: ### Clustered beyond chance? A network with many links per node closes many triangles by chance, so transitivity means more next to random graphs with the same degrees, from `random_reference()`. The dolphins, the characters of Les Misérables and the football teams close from two and a half to five times as many triangles as chance would. The karate club barely does, at 0.26 against 0.24: most of its triangles go through the two leaders, and their many friends would close triangles in a random graph too: ::: {#534216f6 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import polars as pl rows = [] for name in ["karate_club", "dolphins", "les_miserables", "football"]: network = getattr(ec, name)() references = [network.random_reference(seed=s) for s in range(1, 6)] rows.append({ "network": name, "transitivity": network.transitivity(), "reference": sum(r.transitivity() for r in references) / 5, }) pl.DataFrame(rows) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

In a random graph with the same degrees (right), only 85 do, and they are spread about rather than in tight groups: ::: {#10c527c2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} def in_triangles(g): return sorted({ e for a, b, c in g.list_triangles() for u, v in [(a, b), (b, c), (a, c)] for e in g.find_edge_ids(u, v) }) dolphins = ec.dolphins() reference = dolphins.random_reference(seed=1) len(in_triangles(dolphins)), len(in_triangles(reference)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` (121, 85) ``` ::: ::: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#3fc7897c .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} dolphins.plot( highlight_edges=in_triangles(dolphins), show_labels=False, seed=1, width=320, height=360, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: On a directed graph, a triple is a path of two arcs, closed when an arc leads from its end back to its start. A 3-cycle is fully transitive, but a triangle whose arcs all point the same way round from `A` to `C` isn't transitive at all: ::: {#45cebc67 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} cycle = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A")], directed=True ) forward = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("A", "C")], directed=True ) cycle.transitivity(), forward.transitivity() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` (1.0, 0.0) ``` ::: :::
